title: GPU and inference basics
summary: How a GPU executes a model, when work is math-bound or memory-bound, why decode is limited by memory bandwidth, how big the KV cache is, and how batching raises throughput.
outcomes: Explain how SMs, warps, HBM and on-chip memory work together and why GPUs need many threads in flight
Compute arithmetic intensity and use the roofline to classify an operation as math-bound or memory-bound
Estimate prefill time and the decode-time floor (weight bytes / bandwidth) for a given model and GPU
Compute KV-cache size per token and how many sequences fit in GPU memory
Explain how batching and continuous batching trade per-user latency for throughput

lessons.title: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory

blocks.md:
Your GPT from scratch runs the same forward pass on a laptop CPU and on a data-center GPU, yet the GPU is far faster. To reason about inference cost you need a mental model of *why*, and of where the GPU still gets stuck.

We will use one concrete chip throughout: the **NVIDIA A100 80GB (SXM)**, whose numbers are published in NVIDIA's datasheet and performance guides.

NVIDIA's performance guide describes a GPU as three parts:

- **Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)**: the compute units. An A100 has 108 of them. Each SM has its own instruction schedulers, a register file, and on-chip memory.
- **L2 cache**: 40 MB shared by all SMs.
- **HBM** (high-bandwidth memory, the GPU's DRAM): 80 GB on this card, readable at up to 2,039 GB/s.

The model weights live in HBM. Every time a layer runs, its weights must travel from HBM, through L2, into an SM before any math happens.

blocks.title: Where data lives on an A100 and how it reaches the math units

scenes.caption: At startup the weights are copied once from host memory into HBM. After that, inference never needs the CPU for the math.
Each layer's weights stream from HBM through the shared L2 cache. This path tops out at about 2 TB/s on this card.
Work is split across 108 SMs. Each one runs many threads at once, so the chip needs lots of independent work to stay busy.
Inside an SM, tiles of data sit in registers (a 256 KB register file per SM) and shared memory (up to 164 KB per SM on A100), right next to the Tensor Cores that do matrix multiply-adds.
The key imbalance: the Tensor Cores can do 312 trillion FP16 operations per second, but HBM delivers only about 2 trillion bytes per second.

blocks.md:
Software sees the chip through CUDA's thread hierarchy. A **kernel** (a function launched on the GPU) runs as a grid of **thread blocks**; each block is placed on one SM, and its threads can share that SM's shared memory. Inside a block, threads are grouped into **warps** of 32 that execute the same instruction together (NVIDIA calls this SIMT, single instruction multiple threads).

An A100 SM can hold up to 64 warps at once. That number matters because of how the GPU copes with slow memory.

blocks.title: Hiding memory latency by switching between warps

scenes.caption: Simplified, illustrative timing: one warp alone does 1 unit of math, waits 4 units for HBM, then does 1 more unit. Run warps strictly one after another and 4 warps take 24 units.
The SM scheduler instead issues math from whichever warp is ready. While warp 0 waits, warps 1 to 3 start their loads. The same work finishes at 9 units.

blocks.md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

More cores does not mean every program runs faster. If each operation reads a lot of data and does little math per byte, the SMs wait on HBM no matter how many there are. The next lesson turns this into a number.

blocks.question: A kernel is launched with only 20 thread blocks on an A100 (108 SMs), one block per SM at a time. What is the most likely problem?
options: HBM capacity is exceeded
Most SMs have no work, so the GPU is underused regardless of memory speed
The warps are too large, so threads diverge
The L2 cache is too small to hold 20 blocks
blocks.explain: Each thread block runs on one SM, so 20 blocks occupy at most 20 of 108 SMs. NVIDIA's guide recommends launching several times more blocks than SMs. This is a latency or parallelism limit, not a memory capacity issue.

blocks.question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
blocks.explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

lessons.title: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline

blocks.md: Any GPU operation spends time on two things: moving bytes between HBM and the SMs, and doing arithmetic. NVIDIA's guide uses a simple model where these overlap, so the slower one decides the run time.

blocks.caption: Simplified: real kernels also spend time on address math, launches and imperfect overlap.

blocks.md: Rearranging $T_{\text{math}} > T_{\text{mem}}$ gives a comparison of two ratios. **Arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved, a property of the operation. The **ops:byte ratio** (also called the ridge point) is peak FLOP/s divided by bandwidth, a property of the chip.

blocks.caption: On an A100 an operation must do about 153 FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic to keep the Tensor Cores busy.

blocks.md:
Start tiny. **ReLU** on FP16 data reads 2 bytes and writes 2 bytes per element and does 1 operation: intensity $1/4 = 0.25$ FLOP/B. It is hopelessly memory-bound.

A **matrix multiply** (GEMM, short for general matrix multiply) of an $M\times K$ matrix by a $K\times N$ matrix does $2MNK$ FLOPs (a multiply and an add per term) and, with FP16 (2 bytes per number), moves $2(MK + KN + MN)$ bytes if each matrix is touched once.

blocks.prompt: A linear layer with 1024 inputs and 4096 outputs is applied to a batch of 1 vector (M = 1). Guess its arithmetic intensity, then compare it with the A100 ridge of 153.
blocks.reveal: Plug in $M=1, K=1024, N=4096$: about **1.00 FLOP/B**. A matrix-vector product reads every weight once and uses it for one multiply-add, so intensity can never exceed about 1. At batch 512 the same layer reaches **315 FLOP/B**, because each weight byte is reused 512 times.

blocks.title: The A100 roofline: attainable FLOP/s vs arithmetic intensity

scenes.caption: Left of the ridge, the sloped roof is bandwidth x intensity: memory-bound. Right of it, the flat roof is peak math: math-bound. A100 ridge is about 153 FLOP/B.
A batch-1 linear layer (intensity about 1) can reach at most about 2 TFLOP/s, roughly 0.7% of the Tensor Cores. That is the regime of generating one token for one user.
The ridge moved right from V100 (about 139) to A100 (about 153). Here is a hypothetical chip with peak 1000 and 3.35 TB/s: low-intensity work gains only from the extra bandwidth.
Back on the A100: a large square GEMM (intensity about 2,731) sits on the flat roof. Training-style big batches live here.

blocks.md: The NVIDIA guide's own example: an 8192 x 128 x 8192 GEMM has intensity 124.1 FLOP/B. That was memory-bound on a V100 (ridge about 139) and is still below the A100 ridge of 153.
Compare arithmetic intensity with the chip's ops:byte ratio. Below it, speed is set by bytes moved, and adding FLOPs is nearly free. Above it, speed is set by FLOPs.

Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

blocks.question: Elementwise operations (add, ReLU, LayerNorm) are at most a few FLOP/B. What is the standard way to make them cheaper on a GPU?
options: Use more Tensor Cores
Fuse them into the neighbouring kernel so the data is not written to and re-read from HBM
Increase the clock speed
Split them across more thread blocks
blocks.explain: They are memory-bound, so the only lever is fewer bytes moved. Fusing several elementwise steps into one kernel keeps the intermediate values on chip. More math units do not help a memory-bound operation.

blocks.question: A GPU has peak 1,000 TFLOP/s and 4 TB/s of bandwidth. An operation has intensity 100 FLOP/B. Which is it?
options: Math-bound, since 100 is a large intensity
Memory-bound, attaining at most 100 TFLOP/s
Memory-bound, attaining at most 400 TFLOP/s
Exactly at the ridge
blocks.explain: Ridge = 1000 / 4 = 250 FLOP/B. 100 is below it, so the roof is 4 TB/s x 100 FLOP/B = 400 TFLOP/s.

lessons.title: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token

blocks.md: In your GPT, generating text means running the forward pass, sampling a token, appending it, and repeating. Serving systems split this into two phases (the vLLM paper names them the *prompt phase* and the *autoregressive generation phase*; most engineers say **prefill** and **decode**).

blocks.title: A generation loop with a KV cache
blocks.code:
def generate(model, prompt_ids, n_new):
    cache = model.empty_kv_cache()
    # prefill: every prompt token in one pass
    logits = model(prompt_ids, cache)
    tok = argmax(logits[-1])
    out = [tok]
    for _ in range(n_new - 1):
        # decode: one new token per pass
        logits = model([tok], cache)
        tok = argmax(logits[-1])
        out.append(tok)
    return out

scenes.caption: The cache holds each layer's keys and values for tokens already processed (the next lesson covers it in detail). It starts empty.
Prefill runs all 4 prompt tokens through the model in one pass. Every weight matrix multiplies a 4-row matrix, so each weight byte is reused 4 times.
The last position's logits give the first new token. This moment is the time to first token (TTFT).
Decode feeds only the newest token. The model still reads every weight, but uses each one for a single row: a matrix-vector product.
Each further step adds one token to the output and one entry per layer to the cache. Steps cannot run in parallel, since each needs the previous token.
After n_new tokens the loop returns. The time between consecutive tokens is the inter-token latency (ITL), also called time per output token (TPOT).

blocks.md: How much work is one pass? Kaplan et al. (2020) count the forward-pass compute of a decoder Transformer with $N$ non-embedding parameters as about $2N$ FLOPs per token, plus an attention term $2\,n_{\text{layer}}\, n_{\text{ctx}}\, d$ that grows with context length. Each parameter takes part in one multiply and one add.

blocks.tex: C_{\text{forward}} \approx 2N + 2\, n_{\text{layer}}\, n_{\text{ctx}}\, d_{\text{attn}}\quad\text{FLOPs per token}

blocks.md:
Worked example: **LLaMA-7B** (6.7B parameters, 32 layers, model width 4096, per the LLaMA paper; Llama 2 7B keeps this shape) in FP16 on one A100 80GB.

- Weights: $6.7\times10^9 \times 2$ bytes $= 13.4$ GB.
- Compute per token: about 2 FLOPs per parameter, $\approx 13.4$ GFLOP (Kaplan's $N$ excludes embeddings, so this slightly overcounts). At a 4096-token context the attention term adds about 8% more, so we ignore it here.

blocks.prompt: Decoding one token for one user: is it limited by the 13.4 GFLOP of math, or by reading 13.4 GB of weights? Estimate the time for each on the A100.
blocks.reveal: Math: $13.4\times10^9 / 312\times10^{12} \approx 0.043$ ms. Memory: $13.4\times10^9 / 2.039\times10^{12} \approx 6.57$ ms. Memory wins by about 150x, so a single stream can produce at most about **152 tokens/s**, whatever the Tensor Cores can do.

blocks.caption: A lower bound for batch-1 decode; real systems add KV-cache reads, kernel launches and imperfect bandwidth use.

blocks.md: Prefill is different. A 1000-token prompt multiplies every weight by 1000 rows, about 13.4 TFLOP of work for the same 13.4 GB of weight reads. Its intensity is far above the ridge, so it is math-bound: ideally about 43 ms at peak, while reading the weights takes only 6.6 ms.

blocks.title: One request: compute-bound prefill, then memory-bound decode

scenes.caption: Idealised model (peak FLOP/s and peak bandwidth, no queueing or network): prefill of a 1000-token prompt is about 42.9 ms of math.
The first token appears when prefill ends: TTFT about 43 ms. Longer prompts mean longer TTFT.
Each decode step re-reads all 13.4 GB of weights, about 6.57 ms. That sets the inter-token latency and the streaming speed you see.

blocks.md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights, which for example halve the bytes at 8 bits) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

blocks.question: A 13B-parameter FP16 model runs on the same A100 at batch 1. Roughly what is the best-case decode speed?
options: About 78 tokens/s
About 152 tokens/s, the same as 7B
About 24,000 tokens/s
It depends only on the prompt length
blocks.explain: Weights are 26 GB; 26 GB / 2.039 TB/s is about 12.8 ms per token, or about 78 tokens/s. Decode time scales with bytes read, so twice the parameters means roughly half the speed.

blocks.question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
blocks.explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

lessons.title: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token

blocks.md: In attention, the new token's query is compared against the **keys** of every earlier token, and the result mixes their **values**. Those keys and values depend only on earlier tokens, so they never change once computed. A naive loop recomputes them every step anyway.

blocks.prompt: A prompt has 4 tokens and we generate 4 more. Without a cache each step re-runs the whole sequence; with a cache each decode step processes only the newest token. How many token positions go through the model in each case?
blocks.reveal: Without a cache: $4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 22$ positions. With a cache: 4 in prefill, then 1 per step for the 3 later steps, so **7**. The gap grows quadratically with length, which is why every serving system keeps a **KV cache**.

blocks.title: One layer's KV cache filling up during generation

scenes.caption: A 4-token prompt arrives. Nothing is cached yet.
Prefill computes keys and values for all 4 positions at once and stores them. This happens in every layer, for every KV head.
Decode step 1: the new token 'the' computes only its own k5 and v5. Its query attends over k1 to k5, which are read from HBM.
Each later step appends one entry. Compute per step stays small, but the bytes read per step grow with the context.

blocks.md: Size per token: every layer stores one key vector and one value vector per KV head. For standard multi-head attention, the heads together have width $d$.

blocks.tex: \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layer}} \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes per value}

blocks.md: LLaMA-7B in FP16: $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524,288$ bytes, exactly 512 KiB per token. A full 4096-token context therefore needs 2 GiB per sequence. The vLLM paper does the same sum for OPT-13B: 800 KB per token and up to 1.6 GB per 2048-token request.

blocks.title: Where an 80 GB A100 goes when serving LLaMA-7B

scenes.caption: Weights take 13.4 GB. One full-length sequence's KV cache is 2.15 GB (2 GiB).
Simplified: ignoring activations and framework overhead, 66.6 GB is left for KV cache, which holds about 31 full 4096-token sequences (last bar is a count, not GB).
With grouped-query attention using 8 KV heads instead of 32 (the GQA-8 setting), KV per token drops 4x to 128 KiB, so about 124 sequences fit. Hypothetical for this 7B shape.

blocks.md:
Two consequences follow. First, the number of requests you can decode at once is usually capped by KV memory, not compute. Second, each decode step must read the cache of every sequence in the batch, so long contexts add HBM traffic on top of the weights.

This is why Llama 2's 34B and 70B models adopted **grouped-query attention** (GQA): several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the cache. GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) was designed to keep quality close to multi-head attention while cutting this memory bandwidth and capacity.

Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.
KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

blocks.question: A team switches a model from 32 KV heads to 8 (GQA), keeping everything else. What changes most directly?
options: KV cache per token shrinks 4x, so more or longer sequences fit and decode reads fewer cache bytes
Weights shrink by 4x
Prefill FLOPs drop 4x
Context length must be cut by 4x
blocks.explain: Only the key and value projections shrink, which are a small part of the weights. The cache stores 8 instead of 32 heads per layer, a 4x reduction in KV memory and KV traffic.

blocks.question: A server runs LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an 80 GB A100 with 2048-token contexts. Ignoring overheads, roughly how many full sequences fit in the KV space?
options: About 31
About 2,048
About 62
Unlimited, KV lives in host memory
blocks.explain: Each sequence needs 2048 x 512 KiB = 1 GiB (about 1.07 GB). 66.6 GB / 1.07 GB is about 62. Halving the context doubles how many fit.

lessons.title: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users

blocks.md: Batch-1 decode used under 1% of the A100's math. The fix comes straight from the roofline: if $B$ sequences decode together, each weight read from HBM is used for $B$ tokens, so arithmetic intensity rises to roughly $B$ FLOP/B while the weight bytes stay the same.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: FP16 weights (2N bytes), s_kv = 512 KiB per cached token, attention FLOPs and overheads ignored.

blocks.prompt: Ignore the KV cache for a moment (n_ctx = 0). At batch 64, how long is one decode step for LLaMA-7B on an A100, and how many tokens/s does the GPU produce?
blocks.reveal: Math: $64 \times 0.0429$ ms $= 2.75$ ms. Memory: still 6.57 ms for the weights. The step stays **6.57 ms**, now producing 64 tokens: about **9,739 tokens/s**. Batching up to the ridge (about 153) is nearly free for each user.

blocks.title: Decode throughput vs batch size for LLaMA-7B on one A100

scenes.caption: Weights only: throughput rises linearly until batch about 153, then flattens at the math roof of about 23,284 tokens/s.
Add KV reads at 1024 tokens of context: batch 64 gives about 2,732 tokens/s with a 23.4 ms step. Cache traffic, not math, now limits the curve.
At 4096 tokens of context the cache fills HBM at about 31 sequences, giving about 790 tokens/s with 39 ms steps.
Short contexts let you batch far more before memory runs out. Drag the slider: both throughput and the memory wall move with context length.

blocks.md:
Batching trades latency for throughput. In this model at 1024 tokens of context, batch 1 gives one user about 146 tokens/s; batch 64 gives each user about 43 tokens/s but the GPU as a whole about 2,732. Serving teams pick a batch size (or a latency target) on this curve.

The metrics: **TTFT** (time to first token, includes queueing and prefill), **ITL/TPOT** (average time between output tokens), and **tokens per second** across all requests.

Requests arrive at different times and stop at different lengths. With **static batching** a batch runs until its longest request finishes; short requests leave their slot idle and new arrivals wait. Orca (OSDI 2022) introduced **iteration-level scheduling**: after every decode step finished requests leave and waiting ones join. vLLM and most modern servers do this, usually called **continuous batching**.

blocks.title: Static vs continuous batching with 3 batch slots

scenes.caption: Static: A, B and C start together; the batch ends only when A finishes at step 8. Slots 2 and 3 sit idle once B and C finish.
D and E then run as a second batch. All 5 requests finish at step 12; the slots do useful work 61% of the time.
Continuous: D takes slot 2 the moment B finishes, and E takes slot 3 after C. Everything finishes by step 8, with 92% slot use. Simplified: prefill of joiners is ignored.

blocks.md: Decode is memory-bound, so throughput comes from making every weight read serve many tokens. Batch size is capped by KV-cache memory, and continuous batching keeps that batch full as requests come and go.

Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

blocks.question: A service at batch 8 is far below the ridge, and its GPU has plenty of free HBM. Users complain throughput per GPU is low but latency is fine. What should the team try first?
options: Buy a GPU with more TFLOP/s
Lower the batch size to 1
Disable the KV cache to save memory
Raise the batch size (or admit more concurrent requests): each step costs about the same, so throughput rises almost linearly
blocks.explain: Below the ridge each step is dominated by reading the weights, so adding sequences adds tokens at nearly no extra time per step until KV reads or math catch up. More FLOP/s does not help a memory-bound step.

blocks.question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
blocks.explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.
